title: Naming to Learn: Class Incremental Learning with Unlabeled Data
one_liner: When you have new images and their class names but no labels, you can extract good labels from the images themselves by looking at simplified representations and trusting the confident ones most.
lead: Real-world classifiers must learn new kinds of objects over time without forgetting old ones. Usually this requires someone to label every new image by hand. This paper tackles a more realistic case: you have the new images plus their class names, but no one has labeled which image belongs to which name. The trick is to generate and refine your own labels automatically using the images themselves, while carefully trusting some labels more than others.

problem.h2: Learning new classes without labeled data or forgetting old ones
paras: Imagine you trained a model to recognize dogs and cats. Now a factory gives you 1000 images of a new animal, rabbits, but no one has marked which photo is a rabbit—you only know the class name. A naive approach: ask the already-trained model to label them (these are called pseudo labels, guesses from the old model), then train on those guesses. But the old model has never seen rabbits, so its guesses are wrong and noisy. When you train on bad labels, two disasters happen together: you learn incorrect patterns about rabbits, AND you forget what the model already knew about dogs and cats.
This is catastrophic forgetting in the unlabeled world—the model is caught between learning wrong things and losing right things, because the training signal itself is corrupted.

callout.html: Shrink the images down to simpler patterns, use those patterns to pick the best pseudo labels, and weight each label by how confident you are it is correct.

panels.title: 1. The problem arrives
panels.caption: Old model knows dogs and cats well, but rabbit images are new and unlabeled.

panels.title: 2. Naive pseudo labels are messy
panels.caption: Old model guesses rabbit labels. Some guesses are right, some are very wrong.

panels.title: 3. Simplify the pictures
panels.viz_args: Extract key rabbit patterns, remove noise

panels.title: 4. Pick the good labels only

panels.title: 5. Train without forgetting
panels.caption: Model learns rabbits, keeps dogs and cats strong, avoids learning noise.

steps.text: Old model assigns each new image to a class name.
Strip image features down to core patterns only, cutting out noise.
Train a classifier on the simplified features, use it to re-label images.
Give more influence to labels the classifier is sure about, less to uncertain ones.
Learn from weighted labels using squared-error loss; this pushes the model to match the good labels.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: The paper changes how much you trust each pseudo label—which is just a number between zero and one deciding the weight of that training example. For confident guesses, the weight stays high. For uncertain guesses, the weight drops, so wrong labels hurt you less.

hidden.h2: Pseudo-label confidence: which labels to trust
hidden.name: pseudo-label confidence score
paras: The hidden quantity is a number for each image measuring how sure the simplified classifier is that its label guess is correct. A confidence score close to one means the classifier is very sure; close to zero means it is confused and guessing.

The paper estimates this by training a classifier on the reduced features and looking at the size of its output for the winning class. A big output means high confidence; a small output means the classifier thinks many classes are possible.

heat.caption: Darker means the classifier is more confident in its label guess. Highlights show high-confidence images used most in training.

reads.html: You have a bunch of guesses about which rabbit is which. Some guesses come from a part of the model that sounds very sure; other guesses come from a confused part. Trust the sure part, doubt the confused part.
The classifier trained on reduced features outputs guesses for each class (one score per class). The highest score is the confidence. This tells you how much to weight that image when training.

mechanism.h2: Why reducing features and weighting labels stops forgetting
paras: Simplifying the images by compressing features down to only essential patterns works because it throws away noise and outliers that mislead the classifier. The old model's confusion comes from irrelevant details like lighting and pose variations that have nothing to do with what animal it is. When you strip those away, the classifier sees only the real shape of each rabbit, so its guesses become more reliable—because the difference between a real rabbit and a dog is now stark and impossible to miss, so the classifier outputs a clear, high-confidence answer. The model then trains on signals that are closer to truth, not corrupted.

Weighted labels prevent forgetting because the model learns by trying to match labels, and if a label is wrong, training will pull the model away from correct knowledge. By downweighting uncertain labels, you reduce how much a bad guess can drag you backward—the confident labels pull the model forward toward the new class, while the uncertain ones whisper instead of shout. More importantly, downweighting a label that might be wrong about rabbits also means you are not overwriting your knowledge about dogs and cats, since the training force is gentler.

stages.s: Get initial guesses from old model
Extract image features, then compress them
Train on reduced features, collect confidence scores
Weight each label by confidence; train main model
Model learns new class without catastrophic forgetting

math.h2: The squared-error loss with confidence weights
math.words: For each image i, the penalty is the confidence score times the squared gap between the model's answer and the refined label, summed over all images.
symbols: add up the penalties for each image
confidence score for image i (between 0 and 1)
the model's numeric answer for image i
the refined label for image i (a number representing the correct class)
the squared gap—small if the model is right, large if wrong

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Image 1: confidence 0.9, model predicts 2.1, true label 2.0 -> penalty = 0.9 * (2.1 - 2.0)^2 = 0.9 * 0.01 = 0.009
Image 2: confidence 0.2, model predicts 1.5, true label 2.0 -> penalty = 0.2 * (1.5 - 2.0)^2 = 0.2 * 0.25 = 0.05

Image 1 contributes a tiny penalty because the model is already right and we trust the label. Image 2 is wrong but we mistrust the label, so it contributes only a small penalty. Without confidence weighting, Image 2 would contribute 0.25, eighteen times more damage.

math.note: When a label is trustworthy and correct, the confidence weight lets the model learn strongly. When a label is trustworthy but wrong, that mistake still gets downweighted by the earlier refinement step.

bars.h2: Forgetting and learning: naive pseudo labels versus refined labels

charts.title: Naive pseudo labels (bad guesses used at full strength)
rows: Old class accuracy after learning new class
charts.note: Catastrophic forgetting: the model lost 27 percent of what it knew about the old class because it learned from noisy pseudo labels.

charts.title: Refined labels with confidence weighting (this paper)
rows: Old class accuracy after learning new class
charts.note: The model learns the new class well and retains almost everything about the old class because only trustworthy labels get strong influence.

items.html: If the old model has never seen anything remotely like the new class, even its reduced features might not distinguish the new class from old ones. The confidence scores become meaningless.

items.b: Dimensionality reduction throws out important signals.
items.html: If you compress features too aggressively, you lose patterns that would let you separate the new class from old ones. The refined labels become inaccurate, and confidence weighting cannot save bad labels.
If the initial model guesses that most new images belong to one class, the refined labels inherit that imbalance. Even with confidence weighting, the model might learn a biased classifier.

items.b: Done right: use appropriate dimensionality, start from a strong pretrained model, and apply inter-class balance adjustment.
items.html: The paper includes inter-class adjustment to reweight classes that appear too often or too rarely, solving the imbalance problem and allowing the method to work.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small experiment: take a pretrained vision model, freeze it, and train on a standard dataset split into two tasks. Task 1 has labeled images of dogs and cats. Task 2 has unlabeled rabbit images plus the class name rabbit. Measure the classifier accuracy on old classes and new classes after learning Task 2.
demo.metric_eq: Forgetting = (old class accuracy before task 2) - (old class accuracy after task 2)
demo.closing: The demo must show that with confidence-weighted pseudo labels, forgetting stays small (under 10 percent) while the new class accuracy reaches 75 percent or higher. Without weighting, forgetting should exceed 20 percent.
